analysis.evidence: The land (הָאָרֶץ) is the subject and אֹתָם (“them”) is the object. The clause כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב explains why the land could not support Abram and Lot together: their possessions were too great.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third-person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix. The verb precedes its feminine singular subject הָאָרֶץ.

analysis.evidence: וְלֹא נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ says that the land could not support them. The reason given, כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, identifies the land as the territory where they were trying to live together with their many possessions.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ precedes a common noun of both genders in the singular absolute state. The noun is the subject of נָשָׂא.

analysis.evidence: יַחְדָּו supplies “together.” The land could not support both households because their possessions were so great, so לָשֶׁבֶת refers to living in the same place.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לָ introduces the Qal infinitive construct שֶׁבֶת.
analysis.sense: to dwell habitually in a place

analysis.evidence: In לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו, the adverb modifies לָשֶׁבֶת, “to dwell.” The land could not support Abram and Lot living in the same place because their possessions were so extensive.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew adverb with no separate prefix or pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: כִּי introduces הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, “their possessions were great,” giving the reason the land could not support them living together.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew conjunction with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, “because their property was abundant,” הָיָה links the subject רְכוּשָׁם to the adjective רָב. The abundance of their property explains why they could not live together.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, agreeing with רְכוּשָׁם, “their property.”
analysis.sense: to be in a state or condition

draft.change: Add the root רכש and its noun רְכוּשׁ for acquired possessions. The source’s personal-name gloss does not fit this occurrence.
draft.definition: Property or goods that someone owns, taken collectively.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:5 pairs רְכוּשָׁם, “their possessions,” with רָכָשׁוּ, “they had acquired.”

analysis.evidence: In כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב, the singular adjective רָב describes their property collectively as abundant. The extent of their holdings explains why the land could not support Abram and Lot living together.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine plural possessive suffix referring to Abram and Lot.

analysis.evidence: כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב means “because their possessions were abundant.” The extent of their combined property explains why the land could not support them living together.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective in its pausal form, agreeing with רְכוּשָׁם as the predicate of הָיָה.

analysis.evidence: The preceding וְלֹא negates יָכְלוּ, and לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו supplies its complement, ‘to live together.’ Their possessions were so great that they could not live together.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural. The ending וּ marks the plural subject.

analysis.evidence: In וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו, “and they could not live together,” יַחְדָּו describes how they lived. Their possessions were so great that the land could no longer support both households in the same place.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לָ introduces a Qal infinitive construct that complements יָכְלוּ, “they were able.”
analysis.sense: to dwell habitually in a place

analysis.evidence: The closing phrase וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו means “and they could not dwell together.” It repeats the earlier לָשֶׁבֶת יַחְדָּו and explains that their possessions were too great for them to live in the same place.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew adverb with no separable prefix or suffix. It modifies לָשֶׁבֶת, “to dwell.”
